opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd put our ambition this way: we want to build the world that robots learn in before they ever touch the real one.

Right now, embodied AI is bottlenecked by data. Language models had the whole internet to learn from. Robots don't have an equivalent. Collecting real-world interaction data is slow and expensive, it's hard to scale, and it rarely covers the long tail: the strange object, the cluttered kitchen, the drawer that sticks. So the question we keep asking is whether we can make simulation good enough, and cheap enough, that it becomes the main source of experience for robots rather than a side tool.

That means three things.

**Fidelity where it matters.** Not every pixel has to be photorealistic. But physics, contact, materials and articulation have to be right enough that a policy trained in simulation actually transfers. A beautiful scene with wrong friction is useless for manipulation.

**Scale and diversity.** A handful of hand-built scenes isn't enough. We need effectively unlimited, varied environments: different homes, factories, objects and lighting, generated in a way that's both realistic and controllable. Increasingly that means combining generative models with physics engines, so you get the richness of learned world models and the consistency of simulation.

**Closing the loop with reality.** Simulation shouldn't be a closed box. Real-world data should continuously calibrate it, and the gap between sim and real should be something we measure and shrink deliberately, not something we hope away.

If we do this well, the long-term picture is that simulation becomes infrastructure for embodied intelligence, much like data centers became infrastructure for large models. Any team building a robot brain should be able to train, test and stress it in our worlds first. That's the ambition: not just a better simulator, but the place where robots grow up.

r001.rationale: The response describes simulation as infrastructure and a place for robot teams to train, but does not say the company aims to become the global standard.

r002.rationale: It says simulation-trained policies should transfer and that the sim-to-real gap should shrink, but does not state that every instance of embodied simulation should support successful transfer.

r003.rationale: It says any team building a robot brain should be able to use the company’s worlds, but does not identify leading researchers as the intended audience.

r004.rationale: The response does not propose building an embodied-simulation standard collaboratively with other organizations.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. The honest answer is that our ambition is a little unfashionable: we don't think the bottleneck in embodied AI is the model. We think it's the world the model learns in.

When people talk about embodied intelligence today, the conversation jumps straight to the foundation model, the VLA, the data flywheel. But if you look at what actually made language models work, it was a near-infinite, cheap, already-digitized environment called the internet. Robots don't have that. Every hour of real robot data is expensive, slow, physically risky, and often not reusable the moment you change the gripper or the lighting. So the question we asked ourselves was: can we build the equivalent of the internet for bodies? A place where a robot can live ten thousand lifetimes before it ever touches a real object.

That's how I'd define our ambition. We want to make simulation so faithful, so scalable, and so cheap that the sim-to-real gap stops being a research topic and becomes an engineering detail. Three things have to be true for that. First, the physics has to be right in the places that matter for manipulation: contact, friction, deformable objects, liquids, the messy stuff that classical rigid-body engines approximate badly. Second, the sensing has to be right, so rendering, noise, and sensor latency match what the real hardware sees. And third, the world itself has to be generative. You can't hand-build a million kitchens. The environments, the objects, the tasks, even the failure cases have to be synthesized at scale, with enough diversity that the policy can't overfit to the simulator's quirks.

If I'm being ambitious in the way your question invites, I'd put it like this: we want to be the training ground where most of the world's robot hours happen. Not the brain, not the body, but the place where the brain and the body learn to work together. If in five years a robot company tells us they trained ninety-nine percent of their behavior in our world and only one percent in reality, and that one percent went smoothly, then we've done our job.

And I'll admit there's a longer-term thought behind it. Once you have a simulator that good, it stops being just a training tool. It becomes a way to test, certify, and reason about physical systems before they exist. That's bigger than robotics. But we have to earn that by solving the unglamorous problem first: making a virtual cup of water behave like a real one.

r001.rationale: The response aims to make its simulator a major training ground, but does not define the company’s ambition as becoming the global standard for embodied simulation.

r002.rationale: It says the sim-to-real gap should become an engineering detail and describes a 99% simulation/1% reality goal, but does not state that every instance of embodied simulation should support successful transfer.

r003.rationale: The response calls for simulation that is scalable and cheap, but does not identify access for leading researchers as part of the company’s mission.

r004.rationale: The response does not propose building an embodied-simulation standard collaboratively with other organizations.

astra-6.text: I’d define our ambition as closing the gap between what an embodied system can do in simulation and what it can reliably do in the real world. That means building simulation where systems can learn through interaction, make mistakes safely, and develop skills that transfer beyond the training environment. The measure of success is whether that experience helps a robot handle a new task or an unfamiliar situation in practice.

sol-6.1.text: For us, the ambition is to make simulation a place where embodied intelligence can learn, be tested, and improve before entering the physical world. That means going beyond environments that simply look realistic. They need to capture the interactions that matter: how objects move, how actions change a scene, and what happens when something goes wrong. Ultimately, the measure of success is whether what a system learns in simulation helps it perform reliably in the real world.
